title: Conductors and Insulators
lead: Some materials let charge move through them and others hold it where it is put, and almost everything this section says follows from that one difference. It defines the conductor and the insulator, and then uses them three times: to charge a body by touching it with a charged object, to charge a body by induction without ever touching it, once with two spheres in contact and once through a wire run to the ground, and to explain why a charged object of either sign attracts a neutral one at all, which is polarization.
objectives: Define conductor and insulator, explain the difference, and give examples of each.
Describe three methods for charging an object.
Explain what happens to an electric force as you move farther from the source.
summary_html:
• Polarization is the separation of positive and negative charges in a neutral object.
  • A conductor is a substance that allows charge to flow freely through its atomic structure.
  • An insulator holds charge within its atomic structure.
  • Objects with like charges repel each other, while those with unlike charges attract each other.
  • A conducting object is said to be grounded if it is connected to the Earth through a conductor. Grounding allows transfer of charge to and from the earth’s large reservoir.
  • Objects can be charged by contact with another charged object and obtain the same sign charge.
  • If an object is temporarily grounded, it can be charged by induction, and obtains the opposite sign charge.
  • Polarized objects have their positive and negative charges concentrated in different areas, giving them a non-symmetrical charge.
  • Polar molecules have an inherent separation of charge.

figures.original_caption: An electroscope is a favorite instrument in physics demonstrations and student laboratories. It is typically made with gold foil leaves hung from a (conducting) metal stem and is insulated from the room air in a glass-walled container. (a) A positively charged glass rod is brought near the tip of the electroscope, attracting electrons to the top and leaving a net positive charge on the leaves. Like charges in the light flexible gold leaves repel, separating them. (b) When the rod is touched against the ball, electrons are attracted and transferred, reducing the net charge on the glass rod but leaving the electroscope positively charged. (c) The excess charges are evenly distributed in the stem and leaves of the electroscope once the glass rod is removed.

Charging by induction. (a) Two uncharged or neutral metal spheres are in contact with each other but insulated from the rest of the world. (b) A positively charged glass rod is brought near the sphere on the left, attracting negative charge and leaving the other sphere positively charged. (c) The spheres are separated before the rod is removed, thus separating negative and positive charge. (d) The spheres retain net charges after the inducing rod is removed—without ever having been touched by a charged object.

Charging by induction, using a ground connection. (a) A positively charged rod is brought near a neutral metal sphere, polarizing it. (b) The sphere is grounded, allowing electrons to be attracted from the earth’s ample supply. (c) The ground connection is broken. (d) The positive rod is removed, leaving the sphere with an induced negative charge.

Both positive and negative objects attract a neutral object by polarizing its molecules. (a) A positive object brought near a neutral insulator polarizes its molecules. There is a slight shift in the distribution of the electrons orbiting the molecule, with unlike charges being brought nearer and like charges moved away. Since the electrostatic force decreases with distance, there is a net attraction. (b) A negative object produces the opposite polarization, but again attracts the neutral object. (c) The same effect occurs for a conductor; since the unlike charges are closer, there is a net attraction.

exercises.prompt: Can you explain the attraction of water to the charged rod in Figure 18.15?

answer.solution: Water molecules are polarized, giving them slightly positive and slightly negative sides. This makes water even more susceptible to a charged rod’s attraction. In addition, tap water contains dissolved ions (positive and negative charges). As the water flows downward, due to the force of gravity, the charged conductor exerts a net attraction to the opposite charges in the stream of water, pulling it closer.

exercises.prompt: An eccentric inventor attempts to levitate by first placing a large negative charge on himself and then putting a large positive charge on the ceiling of his workshop. Instead, while attempting to place a large negative charge on himself, his clothes fly off. Explain.

answer.solution: Because the charge he places on himself spreads over him and over everything he is wearing, and like charges repel. His body and his clothes are in contact, so the excess negative charge is shared between them, and every part of that charge pushes away from every other part. His clothes hang loosely and are light, so the repulsion between the charge on a shirt and the charge on the body underneath it is enough to lift the shirt away, long before he has anything like the charge he would need to lift his own weight toward the ceiling. The force between two charges also decreases with distance, and the ceiling is much farther from him than his shirt is.

exercises.prompt: If you have charged an electroscope by contact with a positively charged object, describe how you could use it to determine the charge of other objects. Specifically, what would the leaves of the electroscope do if other charged objects were brought near its knob?

answer.solution: The leaves already stand apart, because the electroscope holds a positive charge. Bring another positively charged object near the knob and it pushes still more positive charge down into the leaves, so they separate farther. Bring a negatively charged object near the knob and it attracts positive charge up from the leaves, so they fall back toward each other. An object that makes the leaves separate farther carries the same sign of charge as the electroscope, positive, and an object that lets them fall carries the opposite sign, negative; an uncharged object polarizes the electroscope only slightly and changes the leaves very little. That is how an electroscope of known charge tells the sign of an unknown one.

exercises.prompt: When a glass rod is rubbed with silk, it becomes positive and the silk becomes negative—yet both attract dust. Does the dust have a third type of charge that is attracted to both positive and negative? Explain.

answer.solution: No. There are only two types of charge, and the dust needs neither of them: it is neutral. A charged object of either sign polarizes a neutral speck of dust, drawing the unlike charge in it nearer and pushing the like charge farther away. Since the electrostatic force decreases with distance, the attraction of the nearer unlike charge is stronger than the repulsion of the farther like charge, so the net effect is an attraction. Turn the sign of the rod round and the polarization of the dust turns round with it, and the attraction is the same.

exercises.prompt: Why does a car always attract dust right after it is polished? (Note that car wax and car tires are insulators.)

answer.solution: Polishing is rubbing, and rubbing separates charge. The wax on the car is an insulator, so the charge left on it by the cloth stays where it was put instead of flowing away, and the tires are insulators too, so it cannot escape to the ground. The charged wax then polarizes any neutral speck of dust that comes near, pulling its unlike charge closer and pushing its like charge away, and because the force decreases with distance the attraction wins. The car therefore collects dust until its charge leaks away into the damp air.

exercises.prompt: Describe how a positively charged object can be used to give another object a negative charge. What is the name of this process?

answer.solution: Hold the positively charged object near the second one without touching it. It attracts negative charge to the near side of the second object and leaves positive charge on the far side, which is polarization. Now ground the second object, so that a conducting path runs from it to the earth: the positive charge on the far side is repelled away down the path, or, put the other way, electrons are drawn up from the earth’s ample supply. Break the ground connection while the positively charged object is still near, and only then take that object away. The second object is left with a net negative charge, and it was never touched by a charged object. The process is called charging by induction.

exercises.prompt: What is grounding? What effect does it have on a charged conductor? On a charged insulator?

answer.solution: Grounding is connecting an object to the earth through a conductor, usually a wire. Since the earth is large and most ground is a good conductor, it can supply or accept excess charge easily. A charged conductor that is grounded loses its excess charge almost at once, because the charge is free to move through it and out along the wire, and the conductor is left neutral; if another charged object is held nearby while the grounding is done, charge flows the other way instead and the conductor keeps an induced charge when the connection is broken. A charged insulator is barely affected, because its charges are bound in the structure and cannot move to the wire: only the charge at the point of contact is carried away, and the rest stays where it was put.

exercises.prompt:
Some students experimenting with an uncharged metal sphere want to give the sphere a net charge using a charged aluminum pie plate. Which of the following steps would give the sphere a net charge of the same sign as the pie plate?
  1. bringing the pie plate close to, but not touching, the metal sphere, then moving the pie plate away.
  2. bringing the pie plate close to, but not touching, the metal sphere, then momentarily touching a grounding wire to the metal sphere.
  3. bringing the pie plate close to, but not touching, the metal sphere, then momentarily touching a grounding wire to the pie plate.
  4. touching the pie plate to the metal sphere.

answer.solution: Ask of each step whether any charge is left on the sphere, and of what sign. In (a) nothing is transferred: the sphere is polarized while the plate is near and neutral again once it is taken away. In (b) the sphere is charged by induction, and induction leaves the opposite sign to the plate, so that is not what is wanted. In (c) the grounding wire touches the plate rather than the sphere, which changes the plate, not the sphere. In (d) the plate touches the sphere, and charging by contact shares the plate’s own charge with it, so the sphere is left with a charge of the same sign as the plate. Option (d) is the one to argue for.

exercises.prompt:
A positively charged balloon is brought close to an uncharged metal sphere resting on a stand, whose near side is labeled X and whose far side is labeled Y. What will be the charge at Y (i.e., the part of the sphere furthest from the balloon)?
  1. positive
  2. negative
  3. zero
  4. It can be positive or negative depending on the material.

answer.solution: The balloon is positively charged, so it attracts the negative charge of the sphere to the near side, X, and leaves the far side, Y, with the charge that is left over. That charge is positive, and the answer does not depend on the material, since the sphere is a conductor whose free charges move. Option (a) is the one to argue for. The sphere as a whole is still neutral: what X gains, Y loses.

exercises.prompt:
A positively charged balloon is brought close to an uncharged metal sphere resting on a stand, whose near side is labeled X and whose far side is labeled Y. If Y is grounded while the balloon is still close to X, which of the following will be true?
  1. Electrons will flow from the sphere to the ground.
  2. Electrons will flow from the ground to the sphere.
  3. Protons will flow from the sphere to the ground.
  4. Protons will flow from the ground to the sphere.

answer.solution: Two things settle it. First, only electrons move in a metal: the protons sit in the nuclei of the fixed atoms and go nowhere, which rules out (c) and (d). Second, the positively charged balloon draws negative charge toward X and leaves positive charge at Y, and grounding Y gives that positive charge somewhere to be neutralized from. Electrons are therefore attracted up out of the earth’s ample supply and into the sphere. Option (b) is the one to argue for.

exercises.prompt:
A positively charged rod is used to charge a sphere by induction. Which of the following is true?
  1. The sphere must be a conductor.
  2. The sphere must be an insulator.
  3. The sphere can be a conductor or insulator but must be connected to ground.
  4. The sphere can be a conductor or insulator but must be already charged.

answer.solution: Charging by induction works by moving charge about inside the sphere and then letting some of it leave or arrive, and charge can only move about inside a material that lets it: that is what makes a substance a conductor. An insulator holds its electrons where they are, so a rod held near it polarizes its molecules a little but leaves it with no net charge to keep. Option (a) is the one to argue for. Grounding is one way of finishing the job, but it is not the only one: two touching conducting spheres parted while the rod is near are charged by induction with no ground wire at all.

exercises.prompt: As shown in the figure above, two metal balls are suspended and a negatively charged rod is brought close to them. (a) If the two balls are in contact with each other what will be the charges on each ball? (b) Explain how the balls get these charges. (c) What will happen to the charge on the second ball (i.e., the ball further away from the rod) if it is momentarily grounded while the rod is still there? (d) If (instead of grounding) the second ball is moved away and then the rod is removed from the first ball, will the two balls have induced charges? If yes, what will be the charges? If no, why not?

answer.solution: a) Ball 1 will have positive charge and Ball 2 will have negative charge. b) The negatively charged rod attracts positive charge of Ball 1. The electrons of Ball 1 are transferred to Ball 2, making it negatively charged. c) If Ball 2 is grounded while the rod is still there, it will lose its negative charge to the ground. d) Yes, Ball 1 will be positively charged and Ball 2 will be negatively charge.

exercises.prompt: Two experiments are performed using positively charged glass rods and neutral electroscopes. In the first experiment the rod is brought in contact with the electroscope. In the second experiment the rod is only brought close to the electroscope but not in contact. However, while the rod is close, the electroscope is momentarily grounded and then the rod is removed. In both experiments the needles of the electroscopes deflect, which indicates the presence of charges. (a) What is the charging method in each of the two experiments? (b) What is the net charge on the electroscope in the first experiment? Explain how the electroscope obtains that charge. (c) Is the net charge on the electroscope in the second experiment different from that of the first experiment? Explain why.

answer.solution: (a) The first experiment charges by contact, since the rod touches the electroscope; the second charges by induction, since the rod never touches it and a ground connection does the work. (b) The electroscope is left positive. The positive rod attracts electrons to the top of the electroscope, and when the rod touches it some of those electrons pass to the rod, so the electroscope is left short of electrons and the rod is left with less positive charge than it had. (c) Yes, the sign is different: the second electroscope is left negative. With the positive rod near, grounding lets electrons be attracted up from the earth, and breaking that connection before the rod is taken away traps them, so induction leaves the charge opposite to the rod’s while contact leaves the same sign as the rod’s.

exercises.prompt: Suppose a speck of dust in an electrostatic precipitator has $1.0000 \times 10^{12}$ protons in it and has a net charge of –5.00 nC (a very large charge for a small speck). How many electrons does it have?

answer.hint: The net charge is the charge of the protons less the charge of the electrons, and each of them carries $1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C.

exercises.prompt: A 50.0 g ball of copper has a net charge of $2.00\ \mu \text{C}$. What fraction of the copper’s electrons has been removed? (Each copper atom has 29 protons, and copper has an atomic mass of 63.5.)

answer.hint: Count the electrons the ball holds when it is neutral, 29 for every atom, and compare that with the number the net charge says have been removed.

exercises.prompt: How many coulombs of positive charge are there in 4.00 kg of plutonium, given its atomic mass is 244 and that each plutonium atom has 94 protons?

answer.hint: Work out how many atoms 4.00 kg of plutonium holds, then how many protons that is, and give each of them $1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C.
